newsitem.title: USA: USDA close to announcing 97-98 EEP allocations.
newsitem.headline: USDA close to announcing 97-98 EEP allocations.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department will announce allocations for countries to buy U.S-subsidized farm goods in 1997-98 (July-June) within the next couple of weeks, a USDA aide said Wednesday.
"We would expect to announce (the allocations) on time," USDA General Sales Manager Christopher Goldthwait told Reuters after a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on farm trade.

USDA has not subsidized exports of wheat and other eligible commodities under the Export Enhancement Program for nearly two years. Nonetheless, USDA continues to keep the program on the books in case market conditions change and subsidies are again needed for the U.S. to compete in world markets.

Current EEP allocations for wheat, wheat flour, barley, malting barley, barley malt, rice, vegetable oils and poultry all expire June 30. Allocations for countries to buy U.S.-subsidized dairy product under the Dairy Export Incentive Program also expire the same day.

Earlier this month, Congress cut funding for the fiscal 1997 (October-September) EEP program to $10 million, from an initial appropriation of $100 million, to help pay for disaster assistance for northern U.S. flood victims.

USDA has requested $500 million for EEP in fiscal 1998. But given the budget pressure on other programs, plus the fact that USDA has not used EEP nearly two years, it is unlikely that Congress will approve $500 million, a House aide said.
Thanks to a slightly larger crop, U.S. wheat exports are forecast to rebound slightly to 1.025 billion bushels in 1997-98, from the 10-year low of 995 million in 1996-97.
However, U.S. wheat ending stocks are forecast to remain relatively tight in 1997-98 at 579 million bushels, up from 460 million in 1996-97 and 376 million.

One private sector grain analyst, who asked not to be identified, recently told Reuters the U.S. should refrain from subsidizing wheat exports as long as ending stocks remain below 800 million bushels.
Whether USDA will follow that rule of thumb is uncertain. USDA operated an active export subsidy program for wheat in 1994-95, when wheat ending stocks totaled 507 million bushels.
